lines.text: Welcome to DVDASA with your host David Chips — I mean, David Choe — and the not only sexy and hilarious but award-winning ass, it's Asa Akira. Our very special guest for one more week only is Yoshi

Obayashi. That was super awesome. And on the dark lobes of death, we have Mr. Bobby Trivia. And I guess he needs no introduction — we have Mr. John Cusack here today, who just happened to stop by the warehouse, right? Yeah. So today we're going to delve deep into the myth and the lore of the Culkin Christ.
So I'll just give a little background. Basically, I had dinner a few weeks ago with my friend Julia, and it was the first time meeting Eddie Huang, who you guys have all heard on the show.
And it was also the first night I met John. John stopped by dinner and we all got to know each other. [to Cusack] And how did that happen? I knew your art for a while.
You have? Yeah. Oh, awesome. And I dug it. So you're like fans of each other. Well, I don't know if he was a fan of mine, but I was a fan of him.

I think so. There's a movie John does called Roadside Prophets — I know there's like a million fucking movies he's done, but there's this small one, Roadside Prophets, where he plays a guy with an eye patch. I was probably in high school when it came out.
And it's John Doe and Ad-Rock from the Beastie Boys, and you're at the restaurant and you jump up on the table and scream, 'Free food for the poor!'

I just remember that scene because that was the height of my dining and dashing in high school. You were dining and dashing a lot. I was dining and dashing a lot. And in that scene, I remember you jumped on a table and stuffed as much food in your mouth as you could.

It was based on a guy from the Symbionese Liberation Army named Field Marshal General Cinque. He wrote these sort of English notes to the heiress's parents, and he said, 'I'm quite willing to carry out the executions of your daughters.'

And he would yell things like that. [to Asa] Was your sister in it? No. I love that you guys are in so many things together. I know. How does that work? You get booked for something and you're like, oh.
Well, if I'm producing it, I just hire her. Because I know it's a home run. And I can get her to work cheap. And then sometimes they just ask us to do stuff together.
And nobody's told us we have to stop, so we keep doing it until someone tells us to. Are you close? Yeah. That's so cool. It's so fun if you can do it.

So nobody's told us no yet. [to Cusack] And you have a huge family, right? Yeah, like five. Oh, wow. Are they famous as well? No, but that doesn't matter. No, no, I'm not saying it does. But what's up with this fucking memory? That was a small scene, in a small movie, years

and years ago, and you remember all the detail. Yeah. You probably remember everything you paint, right? No, I don't. You really don't? No, I don't. Sometimes people show me stuff and I go, 'I drew that?' Like at Comic-Con — I drew this kid, you know, Wolverine is one of the X-Men and he can't die

because he keeps regenerating. So I'm like, obviously he's uncircumcised — if the doctor cut off his foreskin, it would just grow back. So I drew this uncircumcised Wolverine for this kid like ten years ago.

And he showed it to me. He's like, 'Hey, remember when you drew me this?' And I'm looking and I'm like, 'That looks like something I would draw.' Really? Yeah. [beat] I remember every porno I've been in.

Really? I remember every single scene. Are you serious? Yeah. See, there you go — that's kind of like Hollywood. It's all Hollywood. We have that in common. Yeah. I remember — I never saw the movie, but you were in one where the premise was interesting, and you tell me if I got it wrong.

It's like — if Hitler's art was accepted, then he doesn't become Hitler. Yeah, that's called Max. That's a good movie. Okay, I gotta watch that. I was trying to remember the name of it. You should watch it, it's pretty good. Is that the premise? Well, no, the premise is basically that

coming out of the trenches of World War I, everybody came back — but it wasn't like today where there's some fake left and fake right, all corporate. There was a real left and a real right. But everybody wanted to go to war. They were into it.

They thought it was a rite of fire, that everything was going to be fantastic, that there'd be some cleansing, purifying moment where they'd become fully alive — fully French, fully English. Imagine that: no opposition to war. Everybody was into it.

And then they all went. It was the first time in history you could kill twenty thousand people in twenty minutes, where technology caught up with human beings' brutality. Coming out of that, I thought, was the coolest period of art that I know of — that post-World War I art. Grosz and Beckmann

and Dix and Klee — all that art the Nazis banned as degenerate art. Right, they would have banned you. Awesome, cool. So it was about the idea that art is basically connected to politics, and always has been, and it has to exist in opposition to the state in order to have any meaning.

Artists are basically antisocial creatures. We're antisocial, but even more than that — shamanistic, too, in a way. So the only thing Hitler did was take the anti-war stuff from the left, from all the guys who came back from battle.

It was fucking wild, crazy, mind-shattering shit. He said, 'I hate the content of this because it's not pro-war, but I've got to steal their shit and put it into propaganda.' He turned art into propaganda. It's about that idea. Was he an artist himself?

Yeah. Oh yeah. Was he any good? No, he sucked. He'd paint these pictures of buildings. Well — he didn't suck, he had skill, he could render shit technically. Technically he was cool, but his shit was — he wasn't able to let out any of his demons, right?
It wasn't his true calling. Well, no — I mean, he turned politics into a kind of black art. If you look at all that shit that went down, they used opera.
They used theater. They used visual arts — all the propaganda. They put all that shit into politics to mesmerize people. So in that way, he was a great artist. He was a black artist.
He was like a black magician, in a way. So the film's all about that stuff. I'm definitely going to check it out. Sorry, what was the name of that movie? It was called Max.
It was called Max. Obviously, I don't agree. [to Cusack] Do you like the art from that period? Any of that stuff? I like pretty much anything if it's good and has some heart to it.
The reason I reference Hitler a lot — maybe too much — is because, obviously, I don't agree with what he did. But he was an artist. And yeah, I've seen his art.
It's pretty shit. If you Google Hitler's art, it's not that fucking awesome. Well, it's interesting — there are no humans in it. It's landscapes. Landscapes, or little dogs.

It was weirdly — it's so weird. It's not what you'd think it would be. No. I mean, it's very weird. He used to draw pictures of dogs in bucolic scenes in old German towns, but there were no people in them.

He didn't like people. [beat] I wonder what Yoshi's art would look like. Actually, we should have an art contest for Yoshi. An art contest, really? I wonder who would win. We should just give Yoshi an art show.

Let's have a DP contest. But you know, if you guys haven't noticed, artists are super sensitive, and Hitler might be the most sensitive artist of all time. He was an artist, that's what he wanted to do, but he got rejected from all the galleries. So when I reference Hitler, it's

usually because — my art, at some point while I'm alive, got accepted. If it hadn't, that would hurt my feelings. That would mean I'm fucking in my studio painting all day and all night, and people don't like this shit, and they say, 'Oh, we don't like your art,' and then I feel

like my second occupation would be mass murderer. I feel like that. And maybe I'm making a joke of it, but I had so much anger, so much — here's the rub, right? Here's why you're a good artist: you let all that out onto the canvas.
You let all that beauty, all that horror, out. I'm gonna buy some Hitler art. No — well, I mean, you probably can't get it, but it's a sick thing to have. But he wasn't able to do it.
So he wasn't a real good artist. He was a thief. He wanted to steal good art. But he had a vision. He created freeways because he thought — he created these megacities.

So if you see the movie, it's very interesting, because he definitely is a deranged artist who achieves total political power. But he wasn't good, because he wasn't able to let his shadow out. He would have been good if he'd let all that stuff in him — let that rage out.

Maybe he wouldn't have taken it out on other people. If David wasn't allowed to paint, he'd probably kill somebody. I feel like that. I feel like that. I remember you telling me years ago — you were telling me, I was like, 'How's it going, Dave?'

and you were like, 'I'm OCD, ADD, I've got this depression, I've got this going on.' And I said, 'Oh, so what are you gonna do?' And you're like, 'Nothing, because I have to be a tortured soul in order to make good art.' Like you have to. It sounds sort of faggy, but apparently it —

you know, this discussion has gone on throughout time, and I've answered it with a question for myself, and I'll just answer it for everyone: do you need to be tortured to make great art? And the answer is: definitely yes. Can you be not tortured and make good art?

Of course you can. There are a lot of people out there who are happily married and have families and create cool shit. But the great stuff — the shit that transcends, that's thought-provoking — the comedy, the paintings, the greatest art, the stuff that speaks to me,

is fucking tortured souls, people in a lot of pain. [to Choe] Do you think that's why you won't allow yourself to be in a happy, long-lasting relationship? My dysfunction is so far gone that I don't even know how to deal with that.
The night's young, right? You don't know for sure, man. The story's not written. The story's not over. Yeah. I think every artist goes through that phase. [to Cusack] Are you tortured, John?
I mean, what I'm saying is — John, sitting here right now, for those of you who can't see, looks like the fucking Unabomber. A little bit. And like you — when I met John, I met —
There you go. Yeah, I've met John only a few times now, so he's a new friend. And whenever I make a new friend, I try to study them and see what they're about, what's going on with them.
And when I met John, I met one of his friends who played Jesus Christ in the movie Bad Lieutenant, the original one. Yeah, Paul Hipp. I love that movie. And Paul's a cool-ass dude.
Just getting to know them, they share my sick, fucked-up sense of humor. And then I met John and I was like, okay, he's into art. I didn't realize how much you were into art and stuff.

And I was like, 'Oh dude, your pal's a fucking — that's a dark dude.' And you're like, 'Dave, I am a dark dude, I'm a sick fuck.' And I was like, okay, so if you're a sick fuck, but you're not as sick when you get it out — that's what I'm saying. So how do you get it out?

How do you get the poison out? Well, I get the poison out through movies. I do the movies and shit, but — I try to do some good ones and get it out that way. But you have to differentiate: if you're an artist, you're gonna suffer,

but there's good pain and there's useless pain, and you want to separate the useless pain from — you're going to suffer. [Choe] Why are you pointing at Yoshi right now? I'm pointing at the collective. If you're going to try to create something, you're going to — [to Choe] Have you always been really dark,

or do you feel like you've become that way? No, I think I was always — I grew up in high school in '80s America, you know, with Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan in a red dress, and the threat of nuclear war, and AIDS. It just didn't seem to me like a real

cheerful place. I didn't feel like I wanted to join a frat club or something. I don't think any artist feels accepted — and even if they get accepted to the VIP club, they don't really want it anyway. Because by definition you

want to try to do things that are new, and when you do new things, it's kind of luck if they're understood at the time. Like that movie Max — nobody understood it when it first came out, and then people are talking about it five years later. That

happens with paintings all the time. So as an artist, you have to get art-time anyway. So you're going to suffer. But, dude — some of that's too romantic, bullshit, I think. A little bit. Yeah, so I call bullshit

on a little bit of that, because you can be creative without having to destroy yourself. Or maybe artists just tend to be self-destructive people. Definitely, for sure. It invites that. The way I look at it: if you're an artist, you've got to have a problem, and if you want to be
a good artist and survive, you've got to deal with your problem a little bit. And your problem is you don't know what to make of the earth — but just to have an outlet to get it out is amazing.
That's why I say it's good for people to do it. It doesn't matter if it's good, it doesn't matter if it's bad, it doesn't matter what it is. Just do it.

Well, for Hitler it mattered. He bottled all that shit up, and then look what happened. Right. I remember at a point when I couldn't make art — because I was in jail in Japan, in prison, facing a seven-year sentence. I got out way earlier than that.
But one part of that scenario was: there's a very structured, orderly way to make art in prison. You have to order the paper, you have to have a pen. I didn't have these things.
I didn't have a pen. You have a time when you can do it — you have a time when you can do it. And none of this is ever explained in English. So I'm just like, what can I do?

You're talking about an Asian prison, too — an Asian person in an Asian prison in Japan. Who the hell knows what that's called. Exactly. So they also give you a specific number of sheets of — like each sheet of toilet paper.
They give you like twenty a day. So I was doing my best to pinch all my loaves really quick so I didn't have a messy shit, and I'd save my toilet papers and draw on them.

Did you already have IBS then? My IBS sort of went away, because I didn't eat anymore, I lost my appetite — that would've been another story. What's IBS? Irritable Bowel Syndrome, bro. I shit a lot. I shit like I'm nervous all the time. Right now I'm not nervous, but inside I'm nervous. Everything makes me want to shit.

Yeah, everything makes me want to shit. So basically, finally, after like two weeks, I got a pen. And I'm like, at least I can draw on this toilet paper — which I didn't know at the time you're not allowed to do. So I'm writing

stuff, I'm writing stories, I'm drawing pictures, and I'm like, 'Yes, finally, this is what I needed.' I was having a lot of emotional nervous breakdowns, and then they do the random room checks every two or three days, and they find it.

They go, 'What the fuck is this?' and wave it in my face, and I go, 'What? I'm fucking drawing.' And they start screaming in Japanese, and I'm like, 'What the fuck is the problem?' And they go, 'You're writing secret messages to the other inmates.' And I go, 'No, no, no, I'm not.'

And they flush it all down the toilet, and I'm like — it's just drawings, how could it be a message? Well, I wrote a lot of stuff, too. But was it important? Oh yeah, the writing — I mean, maybe they just knew the shit was too good to ever be seen.

I don't know. One viewing from the guard — but then it fills me with — I'm already mad they're doing that, I'm already mad I'm in jail, I'm already mad about everything, and it makes me so much angrier. And then one nice guard was like, 'Bro, you gotta get the standard

prison stationery to draw on, and that shit we won't throw away.' So I'm like, 'Oh fuck, thanks for telling me now.' So I got it, but — did he speak English? How did he communicate with you? He spoke a little English, so he was pointing a lot. So then now
the energy and the rage and the pain comes back in a fury, and now I'm drawing like — that shit that was flushed down the toilet, so I have to come up with even better stuff than that.
Did they limit your sheets of paper? No, as long as you kept ordering it and getting it, you could ask for like — Did they let you keep it? Yeah, I kept all of it.
Oh, that's good. Your prison collection. I have thousands and thousands of pieces from there. That's a good show. It's probably worth a lot of money. Didn't you do a show after you came out?
I did a show with it after I came out. In Japan? No, in LA — in New York, actually. I might do it as a book or something. But even now, it's been almost eight years since that happened.
Ten years. Ten years? Yeah. Do you feel like it's still too soon? [to Choe] This guy — like Rain Man with the dates. No, we went to jail same time, same days. I went to jail in LA.

Your jail time crossed over. We crossed swords. No — I always feel like it was five years ago or whatever, and then I'll open a box and find a couple things I wrote, and I'm like, I don't even want to think about that.

It makes me so angry when I — but you saw the Photoshop that Paul and I did of the Culkin Christ, where he played Jesus in Bad Lieutenant, and we Photoshopped Culkin's face on. You got a little obsessed with the idea of Culkin Christ.
All right, so let's get into that. I feel the fire a little bit, because I like to get people riled up, because then I get riled up. So let's get riled up right now.
And then we get to have some fun. Let's get riled up right now. So basically — let's do it — we were at dinner, and that's, like I said, the first time I met John.

And currently I'm working with this producer, Scott Rudin, to develop either a movie or TV show based on my life, and they really, really want me to play myself. But I'm not an actor. And so John's like —
No, there's Larry David. Well, I don't know, I just don't think — of all the things I do, that's probably — I'm not gonna try to do some shit that I — No, and acting like yourself is kind of hard.
I think acting — people, all these people in LA, and obviously John's one of the ones who broke through, but everyone's like, 'Oh, acting's easy.' I think it's fucking hard as shit.

It is hard, yeah. You gotta make someone think you're someone else. You're playing yourself, though. Playing yourself is kind of — I don't know, I think it's hard. Well, you have an acting coach right here.
Well, John said he'd play me with Asian eye makeup. I mean, he already looks sort of Asian. Tape your eyes. Yeah. Or just eat a lot of salt, get puffy. Yeah, get the shit puffy.
And John, for those of you — he looks like he could be half Asian, maybe. A little bit. A little quarter. My mom — people think my mom's Asian. She looks it. We're Irish.

Totally Irish. A hundred percent? A hundred percent. Both sides. Wow. There was that movie, The Atlas — what was it, the new one? Cloud Atlas. Cloud Atlas, where all the white actors had Asian eye makeup.
Oh yeah. It looked sort of shitty, though. It was not good. Why not just use Asian actors? That's like what Hitchcock did — they'd put the eyeliner on the nose. Oh, really?
You're like, 'Oh, I think that girl's supposed to be Asian.' So we started talking about these kinds of things, and John's like, 'I'll fucking play you, whatever.' And so I was hanging out with him.

Well, this thing, Pipe Dream, is based on a person — it's not you, but it could be you. What's Pipe Dream? Pipe Dream's a movie I'm going to make, and it's about an artist, sort of an anarchist artist, who falls in love with a debutante's daughter.

So, you ever see the movie Rules of the Game? That sounds super familiar. Yeah. Is it a black-and-white movie? [to Cusack] How many movies have you made — not that you acted in, but that are your movies?

I know you did High Fidelity, which is — probably like ten or fifteen. Wow. So when you do it — since you could just act in other people's movies — when you're like, 'I want to make a movie,' it's a passion thing.

Yeah, and sometimes it works out, sometimes it's a clusterfuck, and a lot of it has to do with luck and the people you're working with. Do you know while you're making a film, 'this is going to be shit'?

No, there's always usually a pulse. But you can fuck up a movie in three places — writing it, shooting it, or editing it — so you have saboteurs come in in all three phases. But usually it's okay. And now I'll work on

some of the scripts I get — if it's a great script, you don't do anything to it, but I'll work on rewriting it. [to Choe] Do you know anything about the cuckold world? Oh yes, we're producing a movie — we're in the beginning talks, trying to secure the talent right now, having a real

super hard time with it, our star. But basically — you've heard the word cuckold before? Yeah, it's a famous word. So it's about somebody whose wife is being unfaithful, and the guy's a cuckold. But in porno terms, right? No, I don't
know about the porn term. It's pretty much the same, but in the porno movies the guy is in the room while the cuckolding is going on. While the cuckolding is going on.

Supreme humiliation. But the problem is, some guys are really into that, into being humiliated. Well, those are the people who watch the movie. Yeah. So we're finding out that I might actually be a cuckold.
You'd have to have a girlfriend to be a cuckold. I sort of started having kind of — But Dave feels things. He gets jealousy. You don't have to have a girlfriend to get the jealousy.

He wants to fuck everybody, but if they — he says you can fuck whoever you want, but if he asks and delves into questions, then there might be jealousy there. You think that's true, or are the lovely ladies just projecting? We're not projecting — if you check back to the tape a couple weeks ago, you might find

that you were saying, 'I think I am a cuckold.' That's where it came from. We want to make a supreme humiliation movie. I'm trying to think of a movie that would come close to what I'm going for, but I can't. All the best people are losers today,

I think. That's a good — all the best people are losers? Best characters or best people? Just best human beings are the humiliated, yeah. So what's the Pipe Dream movie? The main premise — it's like a Romeo and Juliet kind of thing? Yeah, it's basically like somebody who, you know,

you're an artist, and obviously a sort of tortured soul but a lovable person — which seems to me, for knowing you, right, you've got a big heart, but you're ready to be completely subversive at any minute in many different ways. You're definitely not living the way society would ask you to live

normally. You fit the definition of an artist. Wait, so did you start writing this movie after you met Dave? No. David is a familiar archetype: fuck you Mom and Dad, fuck society. There's a lot of people like David. [to Cusack] You like my acting?

There might not be a lot of people with David's talent, but there are a lot of people like David — lots of artistic people who feel like they don't fit in. So you get some of the extreme versions of that, like a Charles Bukowski. That guy Joseph Beuys, from the '50s,

this German guy — I'm into some of the older art, I'm into some weird shit. So this — if a guy like that, who's far left, like a Che Guevara kind of revolutionary, falls in love with somebody from the far right, the daughter of, like, a Rupert Murdoch, a socialite — and they actually really fall in love, but they're disgusted by each

other. They're disgusted by everything about each other. This sounds like something that would totally happen to you. Yeah, you know what I mean — like if you fell in love with, uh, 'I fucking hate you.'

The daughter of some horrible dictator somewhere who's living in a — I almost killed a feminist. Apart from the disgust, it has to do with class. It has to do with left and right and all the illusions of that stuff.

And it has to do with money and politics. You should star in that, Dave. You guys can trade. But it wouldn't work for me — I have the cartoonish characteristics of a rebellious, starving artist, except I'm the richest artist in the world.
But you could be yourself in this one. Oh, really? I could try to teach you how to be yourself in front of the camera. You're doing a good goddamn job. Really? Look at that.
You're being filmed right now. I know, but this is — it's when they ask you to reenact things you've really done. I don't know, I think that's really hard. Yeah. I don't know.
I guess. It's hard to act naturally like yourself. I know I'm a shitty actor. I told you guys this, but I was playing myself once, and the director liked me so much, and it was this shitty little

indie art movie, and all he wanted was to have me in the background so the main character bumps into me while I'm spray painting, and my only line is like, 'Hey bro, watch where you're going.' That was it. And they did like fifty takes, they're like,

'Dave, can you make it really look like it was an accident?' I was like, 'Hey buddy, get out of my way.' He's like, 'All right, all right.' Maybe you're working with a shitty director. I just — I don't think — it is hard to act. Even just trying to do a voiceover. If you set things up right —
people think I'm lying in my everyday life. Like, how would I act like a genuine human being? Yeah, exactly, I don't even know. [to Choe] So what's gonna happen — is John gonna play you? Oh, no.
So I meet John. You'll be in Pipe Dream, right? Yeah. I'm down with John. John's my bro. So what's this Culkin thing? I try to test John, because I don't trust a lot of people, right?
John's a new friend. I'm like, who the fuck is this guy? I like him, but can I trust him? So I gotta — Does it portray you? No, just in general. Like why — Oh, like in life.
You know, like — I feel like I could steal your car or something. Or your chips. I'm a closed guy, or my chips or something. I'm a closed person. I don't let too many new people into my life.

So I meet John, and then I find out John is into weird shit — he used to hang out with Hunter Thompson. Oh wait, wait, wait, is that right? Yeah, I mean, John and Hunter Thompson were like homies. How did you meet him?
You told me this crazy story that after he died — he killed himself — you were right there afterward, at the scene, and all the bullets were still there? Yeah, it was about a week after.
Yeah, about seven days after he died. His wife was in another room, right, if I remember right? I don't know where his wife was. I think he was calling her somewhere, or something.
But it was pretty intense, because he had one of those — they put him over the stove to get the exhaust out. An extractor fan? So he was sitting there, and he had an American flag in front of him,

and the bullet hit the grille, right in the lip, and all I kept thinking was, he must have planned that, because it was too perfect a shot. And he had the shotgun shells there, and he looked peaceful, and all this crazy shit. So yeah.

So I snatched up a couple of shotgun shells. That's so fucking crazy. Said, 'Fare thee well.' Were you there when they shot his ashes out of a cannon? No, I wasn't there for that. That started to turn into a zoo after a while, because I heard

Johnny Depp paid for the cannon. Yeah, Johnny was tight with him too. Oh, I love his books. It was great. He was a very — he was a Southern gentleman too, he was really loyal, but he was also the greatest bullshit detector ever.

Funniest guy in the room, smartest guy in the room, and understood politics better than anybody — the real, savage heart of the American dream. That was the Doctor. How old was he when he did that? I don't know. I think he was in his fifties.

Fifty-eight, maybe? He had cancer, he was sick, right, if I remember? Did he leave a note? Yeah. Why did he do that? Well, it gets back to the romantic question: did he go out on his own terms, or was he just too broken down to do it anymore?

I tend to say he was an awesome human being and a shaman, a fucking rare, fantastic, glorious creature, but he was also a fucking compound addict, a junkie, and his shit was breaking down, and he didn't want to go out where he couldn't work or
write or do any of that stuff. So it's a little bit of a cautionary tale about the romance of drugs. Were you surprised when he killed himself? Oh, you were? What was your last conversation with him?

Or did he impart anything to you before? No. A lot of the relationship happened on the phone, because — I went to visit him at Woody Creek, and whenever he could, sometimes he'd come to LA and I'd see him.

But that wasn't often, so you'd either have to go out to Colorado. But a lot of it was just on the phone. Right. So all during the first Clinton administration, and up until the first Bush administration, right until he died —

it was basically from about eleven o'clock at night till five in the morning, the phone would ring. Wow. He'd send you faxes and all this shit. His is the type of shit that — I talk about this all the time, when me and Asa get

interviewed for stuff — that it's dead, that type of brave journalism, the spirit of it: to go out and report on things and write on things straight from the gut. All the things he did with Ralph Steadman — go report on stuff, then he writes it, then Ralph draws it.
I love that shit. I sort of want to get back into that — I want to do that with Africa and other places I'm going to go. Yeah, he was a definite original.

He sort of took, literarily, that first-person journalism — well, he started the whole Gonzo journalism. There were some other guys kind of doing it, but he took it to another level: how you experience something is as important as just the facts, right?

So he added editorial into his experience. It's like adding poetry to a history lesson. It becomes more true when you add how it affects you. You become part of the story you're covering, which in a way is actually more honest.
Because there are a lot of people who pretend they don't have all these allegiances. But Hunter was just independent. Nowadays you've got all these people who pretend to be independent, or the left,

and they work on MSNBC or something, and they're basically the White House network. They hire the White House correspondents to come debate about who's going to say Barack Obama's cooler and better than the other.
Right. And they're supposed to be the guys on the left. Right. But Hunter wouldn't put up with that shit. He'd say, 'Barack Obama's drilling people in Pakistan.'
I like people who do that. It's like, fuck it — he just called it as it was. I love that. And not too many people do that, because they're too worried about it.
